stem: Which Italian state was ruled by the House of Savoy and led the unification?

options.content: Piedmont-Sardinia, ruled by the House of Savoy
options.rationale: Correct: it was the one Italian-ruled kingdom of any size.

options.content: The Papal States, ruled by the Pope from Rome
options.rationale: The Papal States were ruled by the Pope.

options.content: The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, ruled by a Bourbon king
options.rationale: The Two Sicilies were ruled by Bourbons.

options.content: Lombardy and Venetia, the provinces held directly by Austria
options.rationale: These provinces were ruled by the Austrian emperor.

explanation: Piedmont-Sardinia, under the House of Savoy, was the only large Italian-ruled state and became the leader of unification.

stem: Who founded Young Italy in 1831?

options.content: Giuseppe Mazzini, the exile who wanted a united republic
options.rationale: Correct: he wanted a united republic.

options.content: Camillo Cavour, the practical minister of Piedmont
options.rationale: Cavour was a practical minister of Piedmont.

options.content: Giuseppe Garibaldi, the leader of the Redshirts in 1860
options.rationale: Garibaldi led the Thousand in 1860.

options.content: Victor Emmanuel II, the king of Piedmont-Sardinia from 1849
options.rationale: Victor Emmanuel II became king in 1849.

explanation: Mazzini founded Young Italy in 1831 to work by popular uprising for a united Italian republic.

stem: What was agreed at Plombières in 1858?

options.content: Garibaldi would conquer Sicily with a force of volunteers from Genoa
options.rationale: That was the plan of 1860.

options.content: Austria would hand over Venetia to Italy in exchange for a payment
options.rationale: Venetia came in 1866 after the Austro-Prussian War.

options.content: Mazzini would set up a republic in Rome under French protection
options.rationale: Mazzini had no part in the agreement.

options.content: Napoleon III would help Piedmont against Austria in return for Savoy and Nice
options.rationale: Correct: the secret agreement of Cavour and Napoleon III.

explanation: At Plombières Cavour and Napoleon III agreed that France would help drive Austria from northern Italy; in return France would receive Savoy and Nice.

stem: Why did Napoleon III make the armistice of Villafranca in July 1859?

options.content: He wanted to hand the whole of Italy to the Pope in return for peace
options.rationale: He did not hand Italy to the Pope.

options.content: He had been defeated at Solferino and had lost the French army
options.rationale: Solferino was a French and Piedmontese victory.

options.content: He was alarmed by heavy losses and by the threat of Prussian intervention
options.rationale: Correct: he stopped before Venetia was freed.

options.content: He wished to unite Italy as a republic under the leadership of Mazzini
options.rationale: He did not wish a united republic.

explanation: Napoleon III feared a longer war, was shocked by the casualties, and worried about Prussian moves. Piedmont gained Lombardy but not Venetia.
hints: Think of the cost of the battles and of Prussia.

stem: Why did Cavour send a Piedmontese army through the Papal States in 1860?

options.content: To restore the Pope to power over the whole of the Italian peninsula and the city of Rome
options.rationale: He wished to extend the king's power, not the Pope's.

options.content: To support Mazzini in the proclamation of a republic at Naples
options.rationale: Cavour opposed a republic.

options.content: To stop Garibaldi marching on Rome and to bring the south under the king
options.rationale: Correct: he feared a clash with France and a republic.

options.content: To attack the French garrison which was holding the city of Rome
options.rationale: He wished to avoid a clash with France.

explanation: Cavour wanted to prevent Garibaldi from attacking Rome (which would bring in the French) and from forming a republic in the south. His army defeated the papal troops at Castelfidardo.
hints: Think of Rome and of the French garrison.

stem: On what date did Italian troops enter Rome?

options.content: 17 March 1861, when the kingdom was proclaimed
options.rationale: This was the date of the proclamation of the Kingdom of Italy.

options.content: 11 May 1860, when the Thousand landed at Marsala
options.rationale: This was Garibaldi's landing in Sicily.

options.content: 26 October 1860, when Garibaldi met the king at Teano
options.rationale: This was the meeting at Teano.

options.content: 20 September 1870, through a breach at Porta Pia
options.rationale: Correct: they entered through a breach at Porta Pia.

explanation: Italian troops entered Rome on 20 September 1870 after the French garrison was withdrawn; Rome became the capital in 1871.
hints: The French garrison left because of the Franco-Prussian War.

stem: Which fact best supports the view that unification depended on foreign help?

options.content: Mazzini founded Young Italy in Marseille in 1831 with Italian exiles
options.rationale: This shows an Italian effort.

options.content: French victories in 1859 and Prussia's defeat of Austria in 1866
options.rationale: Correct: key gains followed foreign victories.

options.content: Garibaldi's volunteers took Sicily with local support in the summer of 1860
options.rationale: This was mainly an Italian effort, with local help.

options.content: Cavour built Piedmont's railways and strengthened its army in the 1850s
options.rationale: This shows Piedmont's own preparation.

explanation: Lombardy came after the French victories of 1859, and Venetia after Prussia's victory in 1866; the French withdrawal from Rome in 1870 allowed its capture.
hints: Which fact shows other states fighting Austria?

stem: Which comment about the nature of unification is best supported by the evidence?

options.content: It was a rising of the whole Italian people against foreign rule from the Alps to Sicily
options.rationale: Many peasants were uninvolved.

options.content: It was led by the Piedmontese elite and involved few ordinary people
options.rationale: Correct: much of the population was not directly involved.

options.content: It was achieved by Mazzini's republican plan without a king
options.rationale: The result was a monarchy.

options.content: It was completed by 1861 with the entry of the army into Rome
options.rationale: Venetia and Rome came later.

explanation: Historians stress that Piedmont's leaders and the monarchy directed unification, with limited peasant involvement; the plebiscites were managed and the south felt conquered.
hints: Think of the part of ordinary peasants and of the monarchy.

stem: Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed King of Italy in March 1861.
explanation: True. The first Italian parliament proclaimed him king on 17 March 1861.

stem: Garibaldi himself became the king of the new Italy after the conquest of Naples.
explanation: False. At Teano in October 1860 Garibaldi handed his conquests to Victor Emmanuel II, who became king.

stem: The revolutions in Italy in the late 1840s failed because Austria and its allies were militarily stronger than the revolutionaries.
explanation: True. Austria defeated Piedmont at Custoza and Novara and French troops destroyed the Roman Republic, and the revolutionaries were divided.
hints: Think of Custoza, Novara and the French in Rome.

stem: Describe how Italy was divided in 1815.

points.description: Piedmont-Sardinia was ruled by the House of Savoy
Lombardy and Venetia were ruled directly by Austria
The Papal States covered the centre and were ruled by the Pope
The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in the south was ruled by a Bourbon king; the duchies were ruled by Habsburg princes

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Piedmont-Sardinia was ruled by the House of Savoy, while Lombardy and Venetia were ruled directly by Austria. The Papal States in the centre were ruled by the Pope, and the south formed the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies under a Bourbon king. The duchies of Parma, Modena and Tuscany were ruled by Habsburg princes.

explanation: One mark for each region described.

stem: Explain why Cavour sought the help of Napoleon III.

points.description: Piedmont had failed to beat Austria alone in 1848-49, so it needed a strong ally
France was the only power willing to help, and Napoleon III had his own reasons of prestige and the gain of Savoy and Nice

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Piedmont had failed to beat Austria alone in 1848-49, so it needed a strong ally. France was willing to help, because Napoleon III wanted prestige and the gain of Savoy and Nice.

explanation: Credit reasons with development.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a letter from a fictional Piedmontese officer to his family, October 1860 (invented for this question)

> We have marched south, and the towns greet us with flags. The people of Naples have voted to join the king. We are told that the whole of Italy is one at last, though I notice that many of the peasants do not know what the vote was for.

**Source B** — a recollection by a fictional Sicilian farmer, recorded in the 1890s (invented for this question)

> When Garibaldi came we thought the land would be ours. Instead came new taxes and soldiers to take our sons. The landlords kept their land. Some say we gained a country, but in our village we gained only a bill from the king.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What does Source A suggest about the plebiscites?

points.description: The towns welcomed the army and voted for the king
Many peasants did not understand what the vote was for

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Compare what Sources A and B show about the experience of unification in southern Italy.

points.description: Agree: both suggest that many ordinary people were not fully part of the national movement or did not benefit
Differ: A describes a welcome in the towns and the vote for union; B describes disappointment, new taxes and conscription

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How useful are these sources for a historian studying the results of unification in the south?

points.description: A is a contemporary letter from a soldier of the winning side, useful for the atmosphere of 1860 and doubts about the plebiscite, but he was an outsider and saw only the towns on his march
B is the view of a farmer, giving the peasant experience, but it was recorded decades later and may reflect later bitterness
Own knowledge: new taxes, conscription and the unchanged position of landlords are well documented; together the sources give two views, but neither covers every region

levels.descriptor: Developed, well-supported explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, using accurate and specific knowledge, weighing them against each other and against alternative views, with a sustained line of argument and a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; limited balance and little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source A is useful because it was written at the time by an officer, and it shows both the welcome in the towns and his own doubts about the plebiscites; but he was a northerner passing through, and saw only part of the south. Source B gives the peasant view of disappointment, new taxes and conscription, which agrees with what we know about the new state's policies and the lack of land reform, but it was recorded decades later and may reflect later bitterness. Together they are useful for understanding that unification was welcomed by some but brought disappointment to many peasants.

explanation: Both sources are invented: an officer's letter and a farmer's recollection.
hints: For (c), consider who wrote each source and when.

stem: Who contributed more to the unification of Italy, Cavour or Garibaldi?

points.description: Cavour: modernised Piedmont, won French help at Plombières, the war of 1859, annexation of the centre, sent the army south in 1860
Garibaldi: the Thousand, conquest of Sicily and Naples, a popular hero who gave the movement momentum
Limits: Garibaldi needed the king's army, Cavour did not plan the south, and foreign powers (France, Prussia) mattered
A supported judgement ranking the two

levels.descriptor: Developed, well-supported explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, using accurate and specific knowledge, weighing them against each other and against alternative views, with a sustained line of argument and a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; balance is attempted and a judgement is reached, but it is only partly supported or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; limited balance and little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Cavour contributed more. He modernised Piedmont, won French help at Plombières, defeated Austria in 1859, brought the central states into the kingdom and in 1860 sent the army south to prevent a republic and to control Garibaldi's conquests. Garibaldi's contribution was dramatic: the Thousand conquered Sicily and Naples and gave the movement a popular base, which Cavour had not planned. But Garibaldi handed his gains to the king, and without Piedmont's army, diplomacy and the king's authority the conquests could not have become part of a lasting state. Both depended on foreign help. I conclude that Cavour made the larger contribution, but Garibaldi made the unification of the south possible.

explanation: Credit a balanced argument and a supported judgement.
hints: Compare what each achieved and how much depended on the other.
